overview: Fiji's cultural history includes distinct iTaukei traditions and the experiences of Indo-Fijian and other communities. Cloth-making, language, ceremony and migration reveal continuing cultural creativity. Earlier chiefdoms need their own histories rather than being collapsed into the modern country.

items.text: Masi is cloth made from paper-mulberry bark. A documented craft workshop shows Mereia Johnston stencilling a patterned border, an example of skills maintained in the diaspora.
Yaqona, also called kava, is prepared from a plant root. It has ceremonial importance for iTaukei and is also shared recreationally by Fijians of different backgrounds.
Fijian, Fiji Hindi and English connect different communities. Family use and contact with Fiji help sustain these languages among migrants.
Christian, Hindu and Muslim institutions help maintain community networks. In New Zealand these include worship, festivals and mutual support.
Indo-Fijian culture developed through and after the harsh conditions of colonial sugar labour. Cultural associations, music and dance sustain connections across modern national borders.

A Lau Islands cloth dated to the late nineteenth or early twentieth century shows stencilled decoration. Barkcloth makers softened bark, beat smaller pieces, then overlapped and fused fibres into larger sheets.
